docs.title: certrally
docs.text:
certrally is a command line client for certificate enrollment with the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP), Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST) and the Simple Certificate Enrolment Protocol (SCEP). It is free software under the Apache License 2.0.

CMP (RFC 9810, which replaces RFC 4210, with the RFC 9483 profile)

  • ir, cr, kur, p10cr and rr with a shared secret or a certificate
  • Keys that the CA generates (central key generation)
  • Requests forwarded by a registration authority in nested messages
  • CA certificates, root CA updates, request templates and CRLs from the CA
  • ping to check a server and mock to run a test CA on your machine
  • Deliberately wrong messages with enroll --fault to test how a CA copes
  • A step-by-step enroll that prints the matching command for scripts

EST (RFC 7030)

  • Enrollment, renewal, server key generation, CA certificates and CSR attributes
  • Authentication with a password, a bearer token, a TLS client certificate or TLS-SRP
  • est mock to run a test EST CA on your machine

SCEP (RFC 8894)

  • Enrollment, renewal and polling of pending requests, also in a later run
  • CA certificates, the CA chain, the next CA certificate, certificates and CRLs from the CA
  • Digest, cipher and HTTP method chosen from the server capabilities, with old algorithms on request
  • scep mock to run a test SCEP CA on your machine

All protocols

  • A live diagram of every message and plain explanations of failures
  • RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519, ML-DSA, composite ML-DSA and ML-KEM keys, also offline with keygen. SCEP takes RSA and ECDSA keys
  • No trust setup: certrally trusts the CA it talks to or the one in --ca-cert
  • Warnings about responses that break the RFCs and a strict profile that rejects them
  • JSON output, capture files and exit statuses for scripts
  • inspect and lint to decode recorded messages and check them

Tested with EJBCA, Nokia NCM, Insta Certifier and the openssl cmp mock server over CMP, with Cisco libest over EST and with EJBCA, Nokia NCM, OpenXPKI and micromdm/scep over SCEP. Tested servers lists how each one behaves.

docs.title: CMP details
docs.text: Getting started shows a first enrollment, a key update and a revocation. This page covers the other CMP options and commands. keys.md describes key types, encrypted keys and DER output, which work the same for CMP, EST and SCEP.

docs.title: Protection
docs.text:
Shared-secret requests are protected with PBMAC1. The request header names CN=<ref> as the sender and <ref> as the key identifier, as RFC 9483 asks.

The shared secret comes from --secret, --secret-file (- reads standard input), the CERTRALLY_SECRET environment variable or a prompt on a terminal, in that order. Other users of the machine can see --secret in the process list, and the shell may keep it in its history.

  • --mac pbm selects PasswordBasedMac for CAs that accept only that, such as Nokia NCM, Insta Certifier and the openssl cmp mock server.
  • --iterations sets the MAC iteration count (default 10000).
  • --hash sha1|sha256|sha384|sha512 selects the digest of the signatures certrally makes with an RSA or ECDSA key: the message protection with --cert, the proof of possession and a PKCS#10 request. With --mac pbm it also selects the one-way function and HMAC of the MAC. PBMAC1 always uses SHA-256. The default follows the key type. CAs refuse SHA-1 unless configured to accept it.

--hash, --iterations and --general-info also apply to revoke and the genm commands.

Requests use CMP version 2, the syntax of RFC 4210, so servers built for RFC 4210 understand them. Only messages that need a field added by RFC 9810 use version 3, such as the confirmation of a certificate that the CA signed with ML-DSA or composite ML-DSA.

docs.title: Certificate contents
docs.text:
Without --subject or --san a shared-secret request asks for a certificate for CN=<ref>.

--key-usage and --ext-key-usage ask for the keyUsage and extendedKeyUsage extensions, as comma-separated lists such as --key-usage digitalSignature,keyEncipherment --ext-key-usage serverAuth,clientAuth. Names are not case-sensitive.

  • --key-usage takes digitalSignature, nonRepudiation (or contentCommitment), keyEncipherment, dataEncipherment, keyAgreement, keyCertSign, cRLSign, encipherOnly and decipherOnly. keyUsage is marked critical, as RFC 5280 recommends.
  • --ext-key-usage takes serverAuth, clientAuth, codeSigning, emailProtection, timeStamping, ocspSigning, anyExtendedKeyUsage, cmcRA or a dotted OID.

The CA decides what the certificate gets. Many CAs take the key usages from their profile instead.

--template-cert device.pem copies the subject, subjectAltName, keyUsage and extendedKeyUsage of an existing certificate, to request one shaped like a certificate the CA already issued. --subject, --san, --key-usage and --ext-key-usage replace the part they set. A kur already repeats the certificate in --cert, so it does not take --template-cert. A p10cr built by certrally carries these extensions in its PKCS#10 request. A request given with --csr cannot be changed.

docs.title: Header fields
docs.text:
--general-info OID:int:N, OID:str:TEXT or OID:hex:DER (repeatable) adds an item to the generalInfo field of the request header, for example a vendor profile identifier that a CA keys its policy on.

--cert-req-id N sets the certReqId of an ir, cr or kur (default 0), which the CA must repeat. RFC 9483 requires 0, so most CAs refuse other values.

docs.title: Implicit confirmation
docs.text: --implicit-confirm asks the CA for implicit confirmation, as RFC 9483 recommends. A CA that grants it repeats implicitConfirm in its response and certrally skips the certConf exchange, so the run ends with the response. A CA that wants the confirmation leaves it out and certrally confirms as usual. The result says which happened.

docs.title: Collect a certificate later
docs.text:
A CA that needs approval answers with status waiting. enroll then polls until the CA decides or --timeout ends, 5 minutes by default. With --poll-later it stops at that answer instead, saves the new key and records the transaction in the --capture file:

certrally enroll --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp \
  --ref device-42 --secret-file secret.txt --subject CN=device-42 \
  --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key \
  --poll-later --capture device.jsonl

✓ Request waiting for the CA
  Status          waiting
  Transaction ID  d503c4aad8beeb7b34b820adb1809771
  Saved           device.key
  Note            Collect the certificate with: certrally poll --transaction-id d503c4aad8beeb7b34b820adb1809771 --capture device.jsonl

poll collects the certificate later, also from another directory. It takes the server, the protection, the trusted CA certificates and the output files from the capture file and reads the shared secret again. A run that signed with an encrypted key takes --key-password or --key-password-file the same way. It polls until the CA decides, confirms the certificate and saves it:

certrally poll --transaction-id d503c4aad8beeb7b34b820adb1809771 \
  --capture device.jsonl --secret-file secret.txt
  • A poll that ends at --timeout while the CA still waits records the new state, so the same command can run again. An enroll whose polling ends at --timeout records the transaction the same way when it has --capture.
  • --server, --cert-out, --chain-out, --key-out, --out-format, --ra-cert and --ra-key replace the values from the capture file.
  • Once the CA issues the certificate or rejects the request, the transaction ends and poll refuses it. After other failures, such as a wrong shared secret, the same command can run again.

docs.title: ML-KEM keys
docs.text:
ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 keys cannot sign, so they cannot prove possession of the private key with a signature. For them enroll proves possession by decryption instead (RFC 9810 section 5.2.8.3), with ir, cr and kur:

certrally enroll --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp \
  --ref device-42 --secret-file secret.txt --subject CN=device-42 \
  --key-type ml-kem-768 --cert-out device-kem.pem --key-out device-kem.key
  • --pop encrypted-cert, the default, asks the CA to encrypt the certificate for the key. certrally decrypts it. Its certConf proves that it could.
  • --pop challenge asks the CA for a challenge encrypted for the key, which certrally answers before the CA issues the certificate.

The CA must offer the method. certrally mock --accept encrypted-cert-pop --accept challenge-pop offers both. --pop with a key that can sign is an error. A p10cr needs a key that signs. The result names the method in the Proof of possession field.

The key is saved in the seed form of RFC 9935, which OpenSSL 3.5 and later read. --new-key takes the forms OpenSSL writes, but not a key saved without its seed. poll needs the key to decrypt a waiting certificate: it reads the file that enroll saved or read. --new-key names the key when it is in another file.

docs.title: Let the CA generate the key
docs.text:
A device that cannot generate a good key pair itself can ask the CA for one (RFC 9483 section 4.1.6). --central-keygen sends a request without a public key. The CA generates the key pair, certifies it and returns the private key with the certificate, signed by a key generation authority and encrypted for the requester. certrally saves it to --key-out:

certrally enroll --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp \
  --ref device-42 --secret-file secret.txt --subject CN=device-42 \
  --central-keygen --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key

Without --key-type the CA chooses the key type. --key-type ecdsa-p384 asks for one. The CA may refuse it with badAlg. An RSA request cannot name the key size, so rsa-3072 and rsa-4096 ask for an RSA key of the size the CA chooses.

  • It works with ir, cr and kur. A p10cr is signed with the new key, so it cannot ask for one. --new-key and --pop cannot be combined with --central-keygen.
  • The CA encrypts the key to the shared secret or to the key in --key. That key must be RSA or ECDSA, because the other key types cannot decrypt.
  • certrally saves the key only after it checked that the signature of the key generation authority verifies, that its certificate chains to a trusted CA and may sign keys and that the key belongs to the certificate. Otherwise it rejects the certificate in its certConf. The result names the authority in the Key generated by field.
  • The key is saved as PKCS#8 like other keys, as the CA encoded it, which may include its public key.
  • With --poll-later the key arrives with the certificate, so enroll saves nothing. poll saves the key to the --key-out that enroll named unless its own --key-out names another file. It needs the same shared secret or --key to decrypt the key.

certrally mock generates every key type that --key-type offers, with 2048 bits for RSA.

docs.title: Forward requests as a registration authority
docs.text:
A registration authority (RA) checks requests before the CA sees them and vouches for them with its own signature. With --ra-cert and --ra-key certrally acts as the RA (RFC 9483 section 5.2.2.1). It wraps every request in a nested message that it signs with the RA certificate, including the certConf and each pollReq. The request inside keeps its own protection, here the shared secret of the device:

certrally enroll --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp \
  --ref device-42 --secret-file secret.txt --subject CN=device-42 \
  --ra-cert ra.pem --ra-key ra.key --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key
  • The CA must accept the RA, usually by the cmcRA extended key usage of its certificate (id-kp-cmcRA). --ext-key-usage cmcRA asks for one.
  • --ra-cert may hold the chain after the RA certificate. certrally sends all of them in extraCerts.
  • The CA answers the request inside, so the diagram shows nested(ir) and then a plain ip. The result names the RA in the Forwarded by field.
  • certrally sends one request per nested message. It does not batch requests.
  • poll forwards its requests through the RA that enroll used unless its own --ra-cert and --ra-key name another one.

certrally mock accepts an RA whose certificate it issued with cmcRA. certrally mock --require-ra refuses requests that no RA forwarded, except a request for an RA certificate.

docs.title: Trust and connections
docs.text:
certrally trusts the CA certificates in the first response from the server and the CA certificates in the --cert file, then checks every response against them. The report lists each certificate trusted from the first response with its SHA-256 fingerprint. If a response does not carry the CA certificate that issued the new certificate, pass that certificate with --ca-cert.

With --ca-cert ca.pem (repeatable) certrally trusts nothing the server sends. Signed responses and issued certificates must chain to a CA certificate from --ca-cert or --cert.

--chain-out holds the CA certificates that signed the new certificate and each other, as far as the response carries them. A certificate that only carries the name and key identifier of an issuer is left out, since nothing protects the extraCerts of a response.

Over HTTPS the server is checked against the system roots or against the CA certificates in --tls-ca-cert. --insecure skips that check, for a test server with a self-signed certificate. certrally then warns that anyone who intercepts the connection can pose as the server. The capture file records it. --insecure cannot be combined with --tls-ca-cert. Over plain HTTP nothing authenticates the first response, so certrally warns when it trusts one.

certrally connects through the proxy that the HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY environment variables name, like other HTTP clients. --proxy http://proxy.example.com:3128 names a proxy on the command line instead, on every command that talks to a server. An https proxy works too. Credentials in the URL are sent to the proxy.

docs.title: Revoke by serial number
docs.text:
An authority that has no copy of the certificate names it with --serial and --issuer. --serial takes a decimal number, hex with 0x or the colon-separated hex that certrally prints. --invalidity-date tells the CA when the key was compromised or the certificate became invalid, as RFC 3339 or YYYY-MM-DD, for the CRL entry:

certrally revoke --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp \
  --ref ra-1 --serial 0x1A2B --issuer 'CN=Example CA' --reason keyCompromise --invalidity-date 2026-10-01

docs.title: Ask the CA for information
docs.text:
cacerts and the cmp genm commands send the RFC 9483 support messages. They are protected like enroll requests:

certrally cacerts --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp --ref device-42 --out ca-certs.pem
Command Answer cacerts or cmp genm cacerts The CA certificates. --out saves them cmp genm rootupdate --old-root root.pem The new root CA certificate, if the root has been replaced. It is accepted only when the old root certifies it cmp genm template The subject, extensions and key types the CA expects. --cert-profile selects a profile cmp genm crl The current CRL. Its signature is checked against the trusted CA certificates cmp genm crlupdate --crl ca.crl A CRL newer than ca.crl. --crl-issuer ca.pem asks for any CRL from that CA instead cmp genm raw caCerts The answer to any info types, given by name or as dotted OIDs

--out - writes the certificates or the CRL to standard output and moves the summary to standard error. --out-format der writes DER, with several certificates as PKCS#7.

docs.title: Check a server
docs.text:
ping sends an unprotected general message and reports who answers and how fast. It needs no credentials, because any CMP answer counts, including the error a CA sends back for an unprotected request:

certrally ping --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp --count 3

  1  error rejection badMessageCheck  ECDSA SHA-256  690 B  12.4 ms
  2  error rejection badMessageCheck  ECDSA SHA-256  689 B  9.8 ms
  3  error rejection badMessageCheck  ECDSA SHA-256  688 B  10.1 ms
✓ The server answers CMP
  Server      https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp
  Answer      error rejection badMessageCheck
  CA says     "message not protected"
  Sender      CN=Example CA
  Protection  ECDSA SHA-256
  Round trip  min 9.8 ms, avg 10.8 ms, max 12.4 ms
  Replies     3 of 3
  Note        An error is the expected answer, because the request carries no protection.

With --ca-cert the answer must also be signed by that CA. A CA that leaves its errors unprotected fails this check.

docs.title: Test how a CA copes with faulty messages
docs.text: --fault NAME makes enroll and poll send a deliberately wrong message, such as a certConf with a wrong certHash or a request that reuses a nonce. Use it against a test CA or with the consent of the CA operator. faults.md lists the faults, the RFC 9483 rule each one breaks and how certrally mock answers it.

docs.title: Enroll over EST
docs.text:
The certrally est commands talk to an EST server over HTTPS. --server is the address of the server, such as https://est.example.com. Add /.well-known/est/LABEL to choose a CA on a server that offers several.

Command What it does est cacerts Gets the CA certificates. --out saves them est csrattrs Shows the attributes, extensions and key types the CA wants in a request est enroll Requests a certificate for a new key, --new-key or --csr est reenroll Renews the certificate in --cert, with the same subject and subjectAltName est serverkeygen Requests a certificate and a key that the server generates est mock Runs an EST test CA on your machine 
certrally est enroll --server https://est.example.com --tls-ca-cert ca.pem \
  --user device-42 --password-file password.txt \
  --subject CN=device-42 --san device-42.example.com \
  --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key

A client signs in with a password (--user), a bearer token (--token), a TLS client certificate (--cert and --key) or TLS-SRP (--srp). est cacerts --bootstrap gets the first CA certificates from a server that nothing can check yet and saves them after a fingerprint check. The sections below describe the sign-in options, the bootstrap, proxies, waiting for the CA and the est mock test CA. Key files, encrypted keys and --out-format der work as for CMP, see keys.md.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text:
• A password over HTTP Basic authentication with --user. The password comes from --password, --password-file (- reads standard input), the CERTRALLY_PASSWORD environment variable or a prompt on a terminal, in that order.
  • A bearer token over HTTP Bearer authentication (RFC 6750) with --token. The token comes from --token=TOKEN, --token-file (- reads standard input, which implies --token), the CERTRALLY_TOKEN environment variable or a prompt on a terminal, in that order. A token on the command line needs the =, because --token alone only selects the sign-in. --token cannot be combined with --user.
  • A TLS client certificate with --cert and --key. est reenroll --cert device.pem --key device.key renews a certificate this way. Without --key, renewal signs in with --user or --token instead, as RFC 7030 section 2.3 allows for certificates that cannot be used for TLS.
  • TLS-SRP with --srp and --user. The password then authenticates both sides over TLS 1.2, so the server needs no certificate and --srp cannot be combined with --tls-ca-cert.

Other users of the machine can see --password and --token=TOKEN in the process list, and the shell may keep them in its history.

docs.title: Server certificate and bootstrap
docs.text:
The server certificate is checked against the system roots or against the CA certificates in --tls-ca-cert. --insecure skips that check for a test server and warns that anyone who intercepts the connection can pose as the server.

When nothing can check the certificate yet, est cacerts --bootstrap connects without the check (RFC 7030 section 4.1.1). It saves the certificate whose fingerprint matches --fingerprint or the one a person confirms on a terminal, together with the certificates it issued. The other certificates of the response are listed with a note and not saved:

certrally est cacerts --server https://est.example.com --bootstrap \
  --fingerprint 9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08 --out ca.pem

--bootstrap cannot be combined with --user, --password, --password-file, --token or --token-file. The request needs no sign-in and the credentials would reach a server that nothing checked.

docs.title: Proxies
docs.text: --proxy and the HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY environment variables work as for CMP. The EST commands tunnel through the proxy with CONNECT, so TLS-SRP and --tls-unique work through it.

docs.title: Waiting for the CA
docs.text: When the server answers that a request is pending, est enroll, est reenroll and est serverkeygen wait as its Retry-After header asks and send the request again, within --timeout (default 5 minutes).

docs.title: Channel binding
docs.text: --tls-unique binds the request to the TLS session (RFC 7030 section 3.5), which works only over TLS 1.2.

docs.title: Server-generated keys
docs.text: est serverkeygen saves an unencrypted server key like other keys, as PKCS#8 PEM with mode 0600. --out-format der saves it as PKCS#8 DER. It cannot decrypt a key the server encrypts.

docs.title: Test CA
docs.text: certrally est mock runs an EST test CA on 127.0.0.1:8443 and prints commands that work against it. It accepts the password of --user (default demo) and certificates it issued. --srp-listen 127.0.0.1:8444 also serves TLS-SRP for the same user. --retry-after answers the first request for each key with 202 Accepted, to test waiting. It generates a password unless --password, --password-file or CERTRALLY_PASSWORD gives one. The printed commands give the password with --password and the token with --token, name the files of --password-file and --token-file and leave out values from the environment. With --token, --token-file or CERTRALLY_TOKEN it also accepts that bearer token with est enroll --token.

docs.title: Testing a CA with faulty messages
docs.text:
certrally enroll --fault NAME and certrally poll --fault NAME send a deliberately wrong message to test how a CA copes. It is the mirror of the fault flags of certrally mock, which test how a client copes. These flags exist to test CAs. Use them against a test CA or with the consent of the CA operator, because a CA may revoke or keep a certificate whose confirmation failed.

certrally enroll --server http://127.0.0.1:8080/.well-known/cmp --ref demo \
  --subject CN=device-42 --fault wrong-cert-hash --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key

✗ The certificate was issued but the confirmation failed
  Error   pkicmp: status rejection, failInfo: badCertId, details: certHash mismatch
  Saved   device.key, device.pem
  Note    The CA may keep or revoke this certificate. Check with the CA before retrying, because a retry can issue a second certificate.
  Faults  wrong-cert-hash (certConf)

A refusal by the CA is the expected outcome. The exit status follows the usual rules: 3 when the CA rejects a request or a pollReq, 4 when its answer breaks the protocol or fails verification and 5 when it refuses the certConf of an issued certificate. certrally saves the certificate in every case it receives one. The Faults field of the report names each fault and the messages it changed. A fault that found no message to change, such as a certConf fault after the CA granted implicit confirmation, shows (not sent). With --json the document holds the same list in faults.

docs.title: Faults
docs.text:
--fault is repeatable. Faults that change the same message combine, for example a wrong certHash in a certConf without protection. "Later messages" are every message after the first request: popdecr, pollReq and certConf.

Name What certrally sends RFC 9483 rule Answer of certrally mock reject-certificate A certConf that rejects the certificate with status rejection None. Section 3.6.1 lets an end entity reject a certificate. Section 4.1.1 asks the CA to answer pkiConf and to handle the certificate as rejected pkiConf. The log notes certificate rejected wrong-cert-hash A certConf whose certHash does not match the issued certificate Section 4.1.1 defines certHash. Section 5.1.2 asks the CA to check it (failInfo badCertId) badCertId, certHash mismatch wrong-cert-req-id A certConf with a certReqId the response did not use Section 4.1.1: the certReqId MUST be 0. Section 5.1.2 (failInfo badCertId) badCertId, certReqId does not match the issued certificate reuse-sender-nonce Later messages repeat the senderNonce of the first request Section 3.1: the senderNonce MUST be fresh. Section 3.5 does not ask the receiver to detect a reused one Accepted. With --strict it refuses the pollReq, popdecr or certConf with badSenderNonce, senderNonce reused stale-recip-nonce Later messages carry a recipNonce that is not the senderNonce of the last response Sections 3.1 and 3.5 (failInfo badRecipientNonce) badRecipientNonce, recipNonce mismatch wrong-transaction-id Later messages carry another transactionID Section 3.1: the transactionID MUST be the value of the previous message. Section 3.5 (failInfo badRequest) badRequest, unknown transaction for a certConf and no pending certificate for a pollReq no-protection A certConf without protection Section 3.5: messages without protection MUST be rejected badMessageCheck, message not protected late-certconf A certConf after the confirmWaitTime of the response Section 4.1.1: a CA that does not receive the certConf in time MUST handle it like a rejection badRequest, certConf after confirmWaitTime. The log notes certificate not confirmed in time

reject-certificate exits with status 0 when the CA answers pkiConf. The report then says that the certificate was issued and rejected. confirmed is false in the JSON result.

docs.title: Faults in a later poll
docs.text:
certrally poll --fault sends the faults in the messages of a transaction that enroll --poll-later left waiting, or that enroll stopped polling at --timeout:

certrally enroll --server http://127.0.0.1:8080/.well-known/cmp --ref demo --subject CN=device-42 \
  --poll-later --capture run.jsonl --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key
certrally poll --transaction-id 5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592 --capture run.jsonl --fault stale-recip-nonce

The faults change the pollReq and certConf messages that poll sends. reuse-sender-nonce repeats the senderNonce of the request that the CA keeps waiting, which the capture file records. A pollReq that the CA refuses leaves the transaction recorded as waiting, so a poll without --fault can still collect the certificate. certrally mock --waiting 1 keeps a request waiting for one poll.

docs.title: Waiting past confirmWaitTime
docs.text:
late-certconf waits until the confirmWaitTime of the response has passed, plus two seconds, because the GeneralizedTime in the response drops the fraction of a second. A response without confirmWaitTime gives no deadline, so --confirm-delay sets the wait:

certrally enroll --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp --ref device-42 \
  --secret-file secret.txt --subject CN=device-42 \
  --fault late-certconf --confirm-delay 2m --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key

Without --confirm-delay such a response ends the run before the certConf with exit status 5. The certificate is saved. A wait that would end after --timeout fails the same way, so raise --timeout for a long confirmWaitTime. certrally mock --confirm-wait 1s keeps the test short.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• enroll --fault cannot be combined with --poll-later, because the first request is the only message that run sends. Give --fault to poll instead.
  • --confirm-delay needs --fault late-certconf.
  • certrally checks each answer as usual, against the message as it was sent.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page enrolls a first certificate over CMP, renews it and revokes it. Enroll over EST and Enroll over SCEP start the same way for the other protocols.

docs.title: Commands and help
docs.text:
certrally --help
certrally enroll --help
certrally --version

enroll, poll, revoke, cacerts, ping and mock use CMP and also run under certrally cmp. The EST and SCEP commands run under certrally est and certrally scep. certrally completion bash|zsh|fish|powershell prints a shell completion script and certrally man prints a man page.

Output is coloured only on a terminal. Output and colour describes --color, NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR and the handling of existing output files.

docs.title: Try it with a test CA
docs.text:
certrally mock runs a CMP test CA on your machine. Start it in one terminal:

certrally mock --secret demo-secret --ca-out ca.pem

Request a certificate from another terminal in the same directory:

certrally enroll --server http://127.0.0.1:8080/.well-known/cmp --ref demo --ca-cert ca.pem --secret demo-secret --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key

The test CA prints the same command when it starts. Without a secret it generates one and puts it in that command. Running certrally enroll without flags asks for every setting instead. The test CA keeps everything in memory, so every run starts empty. Its fault flags make it delay, reject or relax its checks, to test how a client copes. The CMP test CA describes them.

docs.title: Enroll a certificate
docs.text:
With a real CA, a device that has a shared secret from the CA requests its first certificate with an initialization request (ir). --ref names the secret to the CA:

certrally enroll --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp \
  --ref device-42 --secret-file secret.txt \
  --subject CN=device-42,O=Example --san device-42.example.com \
  --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key

--secret VALUE gives the secret on the command line instead, and CERTRALLY_SECRET or a prompt also work. CMP details lists the order and the risk of --secret.

certrally draws each message as it is sent and received, then describes the certificate:

  certrally                                           ca.example.com
  │                                                                │
  │ ir  PBMAC1  506 B                                              │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ │
  │                            ip  accepted  PBMAC1  1.5 KiB  9 ms │
  │ ◀───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │ certConf  PBMAC1  291 B                                        │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ │
  │                                   pkiconf  PBMAC1  637 B  2 ms │
  │ ◀───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │

✓ Certificate issued
  Subject    CN=device-42,O=Example
  Alt names  device-42.example.com
  Issuer     CN=Example CA
  Serial     94:01:1D:E4:EA:C9:F1:25:59:06:0B:13:86:06:94:7D
  Valid      2026-10-13 00:20 UTC to 2027-10-13 00:21 UTC
  Key        ECDSA P-256
  Status     accepted
  Saved      device.key, device.pem

The diagram goes to standard error and the certificate summary to standard output. --quiet hides both.

A certificate the device already has signs later requests. A key update (kur) replaces the certificate in --cert with one for a new key:

certrally enroll --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp --type kur \
  --cert device.pem --key device.key \
  --cert-out device-new.pem --key-out device-new.key

--type cr requests an additional certificate. --type p10cr sends a PKCS#10 request, either from --csr or built from --subject and --san. Some CAs accept only PasswordBasedMac and need --mac pbm.

CMP details covers the other options: key usages and templates, implicit confirmation, collecting a waiting certificate later, ML-KEM keys, keys that the CA generates, forwarding as a registration authority, CA information requests and ping. Keys and output files covers key types, encrypted keys and DER output.

docs.title: Enroll step by step
docs.text:
On a terminal, certrally enroll without flags asks for each setting: the server, the CA to trust, the shared secret or certificate, the names, the key type and the files to write. Flags you give answer their questions. --interactive asks only for the rest:

certrally enroll --interactive --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp

Before it sends the request, certrally prints the same request as one command for scripts and asks for confirmation. The shared secret is hidden while you type it. It never appears in that command, and neither do the values of --secret and --key-password. The questions cannot be combined with --json. With ACCESSIBLE=1 they are asked line by line, for example for a screen reader.

docs.title: Revoke a certificate
docs.text:
RFC 9483 signs a revocation request with the certificate being revoked:

certrally revoke --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp \
  --cert device.pem --key device.key --reason keyCompromise

--reason takes an RFC 5280 reason name and defaults to unspecified. certificateHold suspends a certificate and removeFromCRL releases it, if the CA supports holds. An authority that revokes for someone else names the certificate with --revoke-cert or with --serial and --issuer as described in CMP details. On a terminal certrally asks before it sends the request. --yes skips the question.

docs.title: Trust the CA
docs.text:
certrally needs no trust setup. It trusts the CA certificates in the first response from the server and lists them with their SHA-256 fingerprints, so you can compare them with the ones the CA published. To make sure you talk to a particular CA, name its certificate with --ca-cert ca.pem. certrally then trusts nothing the server sends.

Over HTTPS the server is checked against the system roots or --tls-ca-cert. Over plain HTTP nothing authenticates the first response, so use --ca-cert there unless you trust the network. CMP details covers --chain-out, --insecure and proxies.

docs.title: Check responses against the RFCs
docs.text: certrally warns when a response breaks a rule of RFC 9483, RFC 9810, RFC 7030 or RFC 8894 that some CAs do not follow. --profile strict rejects such responses instead and exits with status 6. Response profiles lists the rules. Tested servers describes how tested CAs behave.

docs.title: Inspect and lint recorded messages
docs.text: --capture FILE records every message of a run. json.md describes the format. Keep capture files private, because the messages of a shared-secret exchange allow offline guessing of the secret.

docs.title: inspect
docs.text:
inspect decodes the messages in a capture file or in files that hold a message as DER, base64 or hex or several as PEM blocks. It shows the header, the protection, the body and the extra certificates of each CMP message:

certrally inspect run.jsonl --ca-cert ca.pem

← kup  run.jsonl:3  ECDSA SHA-256  1062 bytes  2026-10-13 11:02:04 UTC
  Header
    Version          2
    Sender           CN=Example CA
    Recipient        CN=device-42
    Message time     2026-10-13 11:02:04 UTC
    Transaction ID   C0:F1:6D:53:1F:6D:D3:FE:45:E3:D6:E2:2C:BD:DD:8E
    Sender nonce     8B:CD:7D:93:2E:99:E3:0A:91:3B:00:0E:BB:C0:D6:5D
    Recipient nonce  14:09:0A:43:F8:0F:2D:22:A5:74:49:BA:32:61:48:71
    Sender KID       3C:9F:DD:E9:90:36:2B:9D:3B:B9:8E:9F:A1:FB:C5:E4:2C:DF:B1:89
    General info     confirmWaitTime
  Protection
    Algorithm  ECDSA SHA-256
    Signature  valid
    Signer     CN=Example CA
    Trust      chains to --ca-cert
  Certificate response 0
    Status   accepted
    Subject  CN=device-42
    Issuer   CN=Example CA
    Serial   BB:CB:71:D5:56:10:E4:A2:CC:BD:89:CA:90:CC:B9:51
    Valid    2026-10-13 11:01 UTC to 2027-10-13 11:02 UTC
    Key      ECDSA P-256
  Extra certificate 1 (signer)
    Subject  CN=Example CA
    ...

For EST it shows the HTTP exchange from a capture and the PKCS#10 request, the certificates or the CSR attributes. It also reads PKCS#10 requests, PKCS#7 certificate files and CSR attributes saved as files.

For SCEP it reads capture files only. It shows the HTTP exchange, the capabilities and certificates of the answers and, for a pkiMessage, the message type, transaction ID, nonces, status, digest and cipher. The encrypted content is listed with its recipient and size, because only the recipient can decrypt it. The certificates the pkiMessage carries are listed with the signer marked.

inspect checks the signature of every pkiMessage and GetNextCACert answer. Some servers send a CertRep without the signer certificate, so certrally also looks for it in --ca-cert and in the GetCACert and GetCACertChain answers of the files it reads. Without it the signature stays unchecked. A signature whose signing time lies outside the validity of the signer certificate is invalid.

certrally checks a signature with the certificates in the message and in --ca-cert, even when the signer certificate has expired. When senderKID names none of them, a certificate that verifies the signature still counts as the signer. With --ca-cert it also checks that the signer chains to those certificates. It checks the chain at the time the capture recorded the message. For other files it uses the current time. It checks a MAC with the shared secret from --secret, --secret-file or CERTRALLY_SECRET and leaves it unchecked without one.

docs.title: lint
docs.text:
lint checks recorded responses against the profile rules and exits with status 6 when a response breaks one. It reads the same files as inspect, but checks EST and SCEP responses only in capture files, because the rules concern the HTTP response:

certrally lint run.jsonl

A FILE of - reads standard input.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Each release has archives for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64. A binary downloaded with a browser on macOS needs xattr -d com.apple.quarantine certrally before its first run, because it is not notarized.

With Homebrew on macOS or Linux, which also installs shell completions:

brew install misiektoja/tap/certrally

As a container image for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64:

docker run --rm ghcr.io/misiektoja/certrally --help

The image runs as an unprivileged user. To save files to the current directory, run it as your user and mount the directory:

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work -e CERTRALLY_SECRET \
  ghcr.io/misiektoja/certrally enroll --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp \
  --ref device-42 --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key

From source with Go 1.27.3 or newer:

go install github.com/misiektoja/certrally/cmd/certrally@latest

Releases are signed with cosign and carry GitHub build provenance and SBOMs. Verify a download shows how to check one.

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
certrally --version
certrally --help

Getting started continues with a first enrollment against a test CA.

docs.title: Tested servers
docs.text: certrally has been run against the CMP, EST and SCEP servers below. Each section lists where the server differs from the RFCs or needs a particular setting. It also says what certrally shows in that case.

docs.title: EJBCA Community Edition 9.6.3
docs.text:
Tested with a CMP alias in client mode that accepts the end entity password as the shared secret and end entity certificates for signed requests.

  • ir, cr, kur, p10cr and rr work. ir was tested with ECDSA, RSA, Ed25519 and ML-DSA-65 keys. PBMAC1 and PasswordBasedMac both work.
  • EJBCA signs its responses to MAC-protected requests, even with the alias response protection set to pbe. RFC 9483 section 3.2 asks for the same kind of protection in every message of an operation, so certrally warns and --profile strict stops the enrollment.
  • lint found no other deviation in recorded ir, p10cr, kur and rr exchanges or in rejections.
  • Error messages are unprotected. certrally shows the reason and marks the answer as not authenticated.
  • General messages are rejected with badRequest "Can not handle message type '21'", so cacerts and cmp genm fail. ping still reports a CMP answer, but with --ca-cert it cannot check the unprotected answer and exits with status 4.
  • In the tested setup EJBCA signed revocation responses with its ManagementCA instead of the CA that issued the certificate. With only the issuing CA in --ca-cert, revoke exits with status 4 although EJBCA has revoked the certificate. Put both CA certificates in --ca-cert.
  • A cr signed with an end entity certificate is rejected with "Status NEW, FAILED or INPROCESS required" once the end entity has a certificate. Reset the end entity status in EJBCA first.
  • Composite ML-DSA keys were rejected with "Illegal key algorithm, not authorized by certificate profile", even with the composite algorithms listed in the certificate profile.

docs.title: Nokia NCM 26.7
docs.text:
Tested over HTTP with a shared secret and with certificates that NCM issued.

  • ir, cr, p10cr, kur and rr work, with and without --ca-cert. ir was tested with ECDSA P-256, P-384 and P-521 and RSA 2048 and 3072 keys.
  • NCM accepts only PasswordBasedMac. It answers a PBMAC1-protected request with badMessageCheck "unsupported cmp header protection method". certrally then suggests --mac pbm.
  • Ed25519, ML-DSA-65 and composite ML-DSA keys were rejected with badPOP "invalid PoP".
  • NCM needs --recipient to choose the CA and answers wrongAuthority without it. It copies the recipient of the request into the sender of its responses. Give the CA name in the order certrally prints it, such as --recipient 'CN=Issuing CA,O=Example,C=DE'. With the names in another order, signed responses fail with "sender does not match protection certificate subject" and exit status 4.
  • Responses to MAC-protected enrollment requests are MAC-protected, so --profile strict accepts them.
  • Signed responses carry no senderKID, although the CA certificate has a subject key identifier. certrally warns about RFC 9483 section 3.1 and --profile strict stops a signed enrollment with exit status 6.
  • Error messages are signed, so ping --ca-cert can check the answer.
  • NCM answers every general message with the same signKeyPairTypes, encKeyPairTypes and preferredSymmAlg items instead of the requested one, so cacerts and cmp genm exit with status 3. The answer is signed even for a MAC-protected request and its extraCerts do not start with the signer certificate. certrally warns about RFC 9483 sections 3.2 and 3.3.
  • With a rate limit configured, NCM answers requests that come too fast with HTTP 503 and no CMP message. certrally exits with status 2. Wait a few seconds between requests.

docs.title: Insta Certifier 10.0.0
docs.text:
Tested over HTTPS and HTTP with a shared secret and with certificates that Certifier issued.

  • ir, cr, p10cr, kur and rr work. ir was tested with ECDSA P-256 and RSA 2048 keys.
  • Certifier accepts only PasswordBasedMac. It answers a PBMAC1-protected request with an unprotected notAuthorized "authentication failed", so certrally cannot suggest --mac pbm.
  • Signed responses copy the senderKID of the request instead of naming the key of the CA certificate. certrally warns about RFC 9483 section 3.1 and verifies the response with the CA certificate. --profile strict stops the enrollment with exit status 6.
  • A kup carries no extraCerts. Without --ca-cert certrally cannot find its signer and exits with status 4 with a hint to pass the CA certificate. With --ca-cert the key update works and certrally warns about RFC 9483 section 3.3.
  • Only certificates issued by ir authenticate a revocation request. An rr signed with a certificate that cr issued gets an unprotected notAuthorized "authentication failed".
  • General messages are not supported. Each gets a signed error with notAuthorized "operation not supported", so cacerts and cmp genm exit with status 3.
  • Unprotected requests get unprotected errors, so ping --ca-cert cannot check the answer and exits with status 4.

docs.title: OpenSSL 4.0.3 openssl cmp mock server
docs.text:
• The server accepts only PasswordBasedMac. It answers a PBMAC1-protected request with badRequest "no suitable sender cert", and certrally suggests --mac pbm.
  • Its kup carries only the server certificate. Without --ca-cert, certrally cannot verify the new certificate and asks for the issuing CA certificate.
  • The server process exits on cmp genm template and cmp genm rootupdate unless it is started with the options for them, -ref_cert and -rsp_newwithnew.

docs.title: Cisco libest 3.2.0 example server
docs.text:
Tested with the estserver example of libest 3.2.0 on OpenSSL 1.1.1, with a password, a client certificate and TLS-SRP.

  • est cacerts, est cacerts --bootstrap, est csrattrs, est enroll and est reenroll work. est cacerts and est enroll also pass --profile strict.
  • est enroll was tested with ECDSA P-256 and P-384, RSA 2048 and Ed25519 keys and with a PKCS#10 request from --csr. ML-DSA and composite ML-DSA requests get HTTP 400 "Invalid or corrupted pkcs10 request", because OpenSSL 1.1.1 does not support these algorithms.
  • est reenroll works with the client certificate alone when the server runs with -o. Without -o the server also wants a password: a certificate alone gets HTTP 401 and certrally suggests --user. With --cert, --key and --user the renewal works.
  • TLS-SRP works with --srp when the verifier uses a group of at least 2048 bits. The passwd.srpv that comes with libest holds srpuser with a 1536-bit group, which certrally refuses with "server chose the 1536 bit SRP group, below the minimum of 2048 bits".
  • With -t the server requires the tls-unique binding. --tls-unique works. Without it the server answers HTTP 401 "Proof of Possession Mismatch".
  • With -h the server asks for HTTP Digest authentication. certrally signs in with Basic only and gets HTTP 401.
  • With -m the server answers 202 Accepted with Retry-After: 3600. certrally exits with status 2 unless --timeout covers the hour.
  • est serverkeygen exits with status 4. The server declares a Content-Length shorter than its multipart response, so the response ends before its last part. certrally also warns that the response has no smime-type=certs-only parameter, because the certificate part is cut off.

docs.title: EJBCA Community Edition 9.6.3
docs.text:
Tested over HTTP with the CA name in --ca. No end entity was registered for the requests, so no certificate was issued.

  • EJBCA lists POSTPKIOperation, Renewal, SHA-512, SHA-256, SHA-1, DES3, AES and SCEPStandard. scep caps, scep cacert and scep chain work. GetCACert returns the issuing CA and its root. GetCACertChain returns the CA followed by its root. lint found no deviation.
  • GetNextCACert gets 403 Forbidden with an HTML page when the CA has no rollover certificate. scep nextca exits with status 3 and shows the text of the page.
  • A PKCSReq without a challenge password gets 400 Bad Request and one for a subject without an end entity gets 403 Forbidden, each with an HTML page instead of a FAILURE answer. certrally exits with status 3, shows the text of the page and suggests checking the challenge password, --subject and --ca.

docs.title: Nokia NCM 26.7
docs.text:
Tested over HTTP with two NCM installations, with a SCEP CA that issues requests without operator approval and with one that waits for it.

  • scep caps, scep cacert, scep chain, scep nextca and scep enroll work. scep enroll was tested with RSA 2048 and ECDSA P-256 keys, with the default SHA-256 and AES-128-CBC and with --hash sha1 --cipher des3.
  • NCM needs --ca. Without it, GetCACert and GetCACertChain get HTTP 200 with an empty body. certrally then exits with status 2 and suggests --ca.
  • NCM lists AES, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512 and POSTPKIOperation and ends the list with a NUL byte. certrally warns about RFC 8894 section 3.5.2. --profile strict stops scep caps and every command that sends a PKIOperation, because they read the list first.
  • scep chain returns the CA certificate followed by its root.
  • GetNextCACert gets HTTP 200 with an empty body, which scep nextca reports as no next CA certificate.
  • NCM signs its CertRep with SHA-1 whatever the request used, adds no senderNonce and no certificates. certrally verifies it with the certificate from GetCACert or --ca-cert and warns about RFC 8894 section 3.2.1.
  • A CA that issues without approval also accepts a PKCSReq whose challenge password it does not know.
  • A CA that waits for approval answers PENDING with HTTP 200. scep enroll --poll-later saved the request, scep poll --once got PENDING and scep poll collected the certificate after approval. scep enroll without --poll-later polled until the request was approved.
  • RenewalReq, GetCert and GetCRL get HTTP 200 with an empty body. NCM does not list Renewal. certrally exits with status 2 and says that the server may not support the message type.

docs.title: OpenXPKI 3.34
docs.text:
Tested over HTTP with the generic SCEP endpoint of the OpenXPKI sample configuration. In this setup the server issued a certificate for a name in its test domain at once and kept a request for another name pending. Approval of a pending request was not tested.

  • OpenXPKI lists Renewal, POSTPKIOperation, SHA-512, SHA-384, SHA-256, SHA-224, SHA-1, DES3 and AES. scep caps, scep cacert, scep enroll and scep poll work. lint found no deviation.
  • GetCACert returns the RA certificate and the root CA but not the issuing CA, so scep cacert shows the root as the issuing CA.
  • A pending request gets a PENDING CertRep with HTTP 202 Accepted. certrally treats it as any PENDING answer and saves the state file. scep poll --once gets PENDING with HTTP 202 again.
  • A PKCSReq with a wrong challenge password is kept pending as well, not refused, so scep enroll polls until --timeout.
  • A RenewalReq gets a FAILURE CertRep with badCertId and HTTP 400 Bad Request, although the server lists Renewal. certrally exits with status 3 and suggests --pkcsreq. scep renew --pkcsreq works without a challenge password. In this setup the new certificate kept the end date of the old one.
  • inspect verifies the signatures of the requests and of the CertReps, which the RA certificate signs.
  • GetCACertChain gets 400 Bad Request "Unknown operation" and GetNextCACert gets 500 Internal Server Error. scep chain and scep nextca exit with status 3.

docs.title: micromdm/scep 2.3.0
docs.text:
Tested with the scepserver of micromdm/scep 2.3.0 with a challenge password and -allowrenew 0.

  • scep caps, scep cacert, scep enroll and scep renew work. scep enroll was tested with RSA 2048 and ECDSA P-256 keys, with the default SHA-256 and AES-128-CBC and with --hash sha1 --cipher des3. lint found no deviation.
  • The server encrypts every CertRep with single DES, whatever the request used. Without --allow-des certrally exits with status 4 and suggests the flag.
  • The server checks the challenge password in a RenewalReq as well, so scep renew needs --challenge or --challenge-file. Without it the renewal gets FAILURE with badRequest.
  • GetCACertChain, GetNextCACert, GetCert and GetCRL get HTTP 500 "not implemented", so scep chain, scep nextca, scep getcert and scep getcrl exit with status 3.

docs.title: JSON output and capture files
docs.text:
certrally can describe its work in JSON for scripts. It can also record the CMP, EST and SCEP messages of a run for later inspection.

  • --json prints the outcome of one command as a JSON document on standard output.
  • --capture FILE appends every message of a run, with its bytes, to a JSON Lines file.

Later versions may add fields. Existing fields keep their names and meaning.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Names are RFC 4514 strings, such as CN=device-42,O=Example, with the attributes in their encoded order. Attribute types other than CN, O, OU, C, L, ST, STREET, POSTALCODE, SERIALNUMBER, UID and DC appear as dotted OIDs.
  • Times are RFC 3339 in UTC.
  • Message bytes and info type values are base64. Transaction IDs, key identifiers, SCEP nonces and fingerprints are lower-case hex. A SCEP transaction ID is the string of the message, which certrally sends as 40 upper-case hex digits. Certificate serial numbers are upper-case hex.
  • Certificates, CRLs, public keys and requests are PEM strings. Private keys never appear in JSON output or capture files.
  • Text from the server, such as statusText, is kept as the server sent it.

docs.title: JSON output
docs.text:
--json works with enroll, poll, revoke, cacerts, cmp genm and its subcommands, ping, inspect, lint, keygen, the est commands except est mock and the scep commands except scep mock. Standard output then holds exactly one JSON document, whatever the outcome. The ladder diagram and the text report are not printed. The exit status is the same as without --json.

When certrally cannot parse the command line, for example because of an unknown flag or a missing required flag, the document holds the error and the error is also printed on standard error. --json cannot be combined with --quiet or with an output file of -.

certrally enroll --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp --ref device-42 \
  --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key --json | jq -r .result.certificate.notAfter

docs.title: Document
Message records
docs.text: Field Meaning kind request, response, failure or connect. A failure is a request that got no HTTP response, or an EST connection that failed. A connect record describes a TLS connection of an EST command time When the request was sent or the response or failure arrived elapsedMs Round-trip time of a response or failure in milliseconds httpStatus, contentType The HTTP status and content type of a response size Body size in bytes body The PKIBody type, such as ir, ip, genp or error. Absent when the body is not a CMP message nested The body types of the messages in a nested body, such as ["ir"] for a request that a registration authority forwards protection The protection algorithm, such as PBMAC1 or ML-DSA-65. It is none for an unprotected message sender The sender name in the header transactionId, senderKid Header fields, as hex status, failInfo, statusText The first PKIStatusInfo of an ip, cp, kup, rp or error body. failInfo lists the failure bit names. For SCEP, the pkiStatus of a CertRep, SUCCESS, PENDING or FAILURE, and the failInfo name checkAfter The seconds a pollRep asks the client to wait extraCerts The number of certificates in extraCerts method, path, operation The HTTP method and path of an EST request and its EST operation, such as simpleenroll. A SCEP request has the method and its SCEP operation, such as GetCACert or PKIOperation. Responses also carry operation caName The CA name that a SCEP request sends in its message parameter messageType, senderNonce, recipientNonce The message type of a SCEP pkiMessage, such as PKCSReq or CertRep, and its nonces digest, cipher The signature digest and the content cipher of a SCEP pkiMessage, such as SHA-256 and AES-128-CBC capabilities The capabilities of a SCEP GetCACaps answer content The EST message in the body: pkcs10, certs-only, csrattrs or serverkeygen. Absent for a body that is not one of them, such as an error subject The subject of an EST PKCS#10 request certificates The number of certificates in an EST certs-only response, in the certificate part of a serverkeygen response or in a SCEP certificate answer retryAfter The seconds the Retry-After header of an EST or SCEP response asks for parts The parts of an EST serverkeygen response, each with contentType and size. The key part is never decoded or stored text The text of an EST or SCEP error response, as the server sent it. For a SCEP error page in HTML, the text of the page without its markup tls The connection of a connect record: version, cipherSuite, server with the subject of the server certificate and srpUser for a TLS-SRP sign-in problem Why a response cannot be a CMP, EST or SCEP answer (for example HTTP 404 Not Found), why its EST message does not decode or why a request failed der The message bytes. For EST, the decoded body, and for serverkeygen only its certificate part. For SCEP, the pkiMessage of a request, also when it travels in the URL, or the body of a response. Only capture files include them

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Field Meaning title One line that says what failed, as in the text report message The underlying error status, failInfo, statusText The CA status of a rejection httpStatus, retryAfter The HTTP status and Retry-After seconds of an EST or SCEP refusal. statusText then holds the text of the server unauthenticated true when certrally could not verify the rejection, so any peer on the path could have sent it hint What to check or change, when certrally can tell note More context, such as advice for an issued but unconfirmed certificate

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A certificate in a result has subject, issuer, serial, notBefore, notAfter, altNames, key, sha256 and pem. A command run under cmp, such as cmp enroll, has the result of the same command without the prefix.

Command Result fields enroll, poll status, confirmed, implicitConfirm, certificate, chain, saved, transactionId. With exit status 5 the result is present and confirmed is false. confirmed is also false after --fault reject-certificate, which rejects the certificate. implicitConfirm is true when the CA granted implicit confirmation, so no certConf was sent. proofOfPossession is encrypted-cert or challenge for a key that cannot sign, such as an ML-KEM key, and absent otherwise. centralKeyGeneration is true and keyGenerationAuthority names the signer of the key when the CA generated the key with --central-keygen. Both are absent otherwise. registrationAuthority is the subject of the --ra-cert certificate that forwarded the requests, absent without one. When the CA keeps the request waiting, under enroll --poll-later or when polling ends at --timeout with --capture, status is waiting, certificate is null, saved lists only a new key and nextPoll tells when the CA asked for the next poll, if it did revoke certificate, issuer, serial, reason, invalidityDate. certificate is null when the certificate was named with --serial and --issuer. invalidityDate is present when --invalidity-date was given cacerts, cmp genm cacerts certificates, saved cmp genm rootupdate update with newWithNew, newWithOld and oldWithNew. It is null when no update is available. saved cmp genm template template with subject, extensions and keyTypes. It is null when the CA imposes nothing. An attribute without a value in subject is one the requester fills in. Each extension has oid, name and critical cmp genm crl, cmp genm crlupdate crl with issuer, thisUpdate, nextUpdate, number, revoked, signature and pem. It is null when there is none. signature is valid, invalid or unchecked. saved cmp genm raw items, each with infoType, oid and value ping sent, answered, sender, protection, rttMs with min, avg and max. With --ca-cert, verified tells whether every answer was signed by that CA keygen keyType, key, publicKey, csr, saved. With --list, keyTypes est cacerts certificates, saved and verified, which says how the certificates were checked: tls by the TLS certificate of the server, srp by a TLS-SRP sign-in, fingerprint by
