docs.title: Capture files
docs.text:
--capture FILE works with every command that talks to a server. It appends the run to FILE as JSON Lines, one JSON object per line:

  1. A start line with format (currently 1), tool, version, command, server and time. A run of an EST or SCEP command adds protocol with the value est or scep. A run with --insecure adds insecure with the value true, because it did not check the TLS certificate of the server.
  2. One message record per request, response, failure or EST connection, including der.
  3. A transaction line with time, id, state and resume when the run leaves a waiting transaction for poll (state is waiting) or poll ends one (ended). id is the transaction ID. resume holds what poll needs: the server, the protection settings and the names of their files, the trusted CA certificates, the output files with their format, the name of the key file when the CA encrypts the certificate for the key and the state of the CMP transaction. It holds no secret or private key. poll uses the last line of a transaction.
  4. An end line with time and exitStatus.

Each run appends its own lines, so one file can hold several runs. Readers should skip lines of other kinds, which later versions may add. --capture works together with --json and --quiet. certrally inspect and certrally lint read capture files.

certrally creates the file with mode 0600. Keep capture files private: anyone who has the messages of a MAC-protected exchange can try to guess the shared secret offline.

docs.title: Keys and output files
docs.text: These options work the same for the CMP, EST and SCEP commands. The SCEP commands generate only RSA and ECDSA keys, and their --key must be RSA.

docs.title: Key files
docs.text:
certrally writes private keys as unencrypted PKCS#8 PEM with mode 0600. certrally keygen --list prints the key types.

--key and --new-key also take an encrypted PKCS#8 key, as openssl pkcs8 -topk8 writes it (PBES2 with PBKDF2 and AES). The password comes from --key-password, --key-password-file (- reads standard input), the CERTRALLY_KEY_PASSWORD environment variable or a prompt on a terminal, in that order. Other users of the machine can see --key-password in the process list. A key encrypted the older way, with Proc-Type headers in the PEM file, is not supported. This command converts one:

openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -in old.key -out device.p8

docs.title: Generate a key offline
docs.text:
keygen creates a key without contacting a CA, for example to send a PKCS#10 request through another channel:

certrally keygen --key-type ml-dsa-65 --out device.key \
  --csr-out device.csr --subject CN=device-42 --san device-42.example.com

--pub-out also saves the public key. An ML-KEM key cannot sign a request, so --csr-out does not work with --key-type ml-kem-768 or ml-kem-1024.

docs.title: DER output
docs.text: --out-format der writes the output files as DER instead of PEM. A certificate, a PKCS#8 key, a public key, a request and a CRL are written as is. A file that holds several certificates, such as --chain-out and the --out of cacerts, est cacerts and scep cacert, becomes PKCS#7. poll keeps the format of the enroll run unless its own --out-format replaces it. The default is pem.

docs.title: The CMP test CA
docs.text: Getting started introduces certrally mock, a CMP test CA for trying certrally and test scripts without a real CA. This page describes what it does and the fault flags that make it delay, reject or confirm requests differently and accept deviations from RFC 9483, to test how a client copes. To test a CA the other way around, certrally enroll --fault and poll --fault send deliberately wrong messages. faults.md describes them and how the test CA answers each one.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
certrally mock listens on 127.0.0.1:8080 (--listen) and answers at /.well-known/cmp. It issues certificates for ir, cr, kur and p10cr, confirms and revokes them and answers the requests for CA certificates, a request template and CRLs. It accepts the shared secret for --ref (default demo) and signatures made with certificates it issued. It copies the requested subject and extensions, such as subjectAltName and extendedKeyUsage, into the certificate, but always sets keyUsage to digitalSignature. For enroll --central-keygen it generates the key pair. That is ECDSA P-256 when the request leaves the choice to it and otherwise any type that --key-type offers, with 2048 bits for RSA. A key generation authority certificate that it issues at startup with the id-kp-cmKGA extended key usage signs the private key. It accepts requests that a registration authority forwards. The secret comes from --secret, --secret-file or CERTRALLY_SECRET. Without any of them, a random secret is generated and printed. --ca-out saves the CA certificate for --ca-cert. Everything lives in memory and is lost when the CA stops.

The startup report shows the address, the CA name, the secret source and the fault flags in use, then an enroll command that works against the CA. The command gives the secret with --secret, names the file of --secret-file and leaves out a secret from CERTRALLY_SECRET. Every request is logged on one line: the time, the request body and its protection, the response and how long it took. A response with a statusString adds it in quotes, such as the reason the CA refused a request. A revocation adds a line below its request with the serial number, the reason and the invalidity date when the request gave one. A generated key pair adds a line with its key type. A forwarded request adds a line with the subject of the registration authority. A certConf that rejects the certificate adds a certificate rejected line and a certificate whose certConf came too late a certificate not confirmed in time line, each with the serial number. The CRL lists the invalidity date too.

docs.title: Registration authorities
docs.text:
The test CA accepts a request that a registration authority (RA) forwards in a nested message, as enroll --ra-cert and --ra-key send it. The RA must sign the nested message with a certificate that the CA issued with the cmcRA extended key usage and has not revoked. Enroll one with --ext-key-usage cmcRA:

certrally enroll --server http://127.0.0.1:8080/.well-known/cmp --ref demo \
  --subject CN=ra --ext-key-usage cmcRA --cert-out ra.pem --key-out ra.key

Other RAs are refused with notAuthorized and a MAC-protected nested message with wrongIntegrity. Requests that no RA forwarded are accepted as usual. --require-ra refuses those with notAuthorized, except a request for a certificate with cmcRA, so that an RA can enroll.

certrally mock --require-ra

docs.title: Delayed answers
docs.text:
--waiting N answers each certificate and revocation request with status waiting and decides it on the Nth poll. --check-after sets the time the response tells the client to wait before it polls (default 1s). certrally polls when asked and waits at least one second between polls. enroll --poll-later and poll collect the certificate in a later run.

certrally mock --waiting 2 --check-after 5s

docs.title: Rejections
docs.text:
--reject FAILINFO[:TEXT] rejects every certificate and revocation request with the given failInfo and an optional statusString. With --waiting the rejection comes on the last poll.

certrally mock --reject badCertTemplate:'subject not allowed'

The failInfo names are those of RFC 9810 section 5.2.3, such as badRequest, badCertTemplate, badPOP or systemUnavail. Shell completion lists them.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
--grant-implicit-confirm grants implicit confirmation to a request that asks for it, so that the client need not send certConf. A request that does not ask for it is confirmed as usual. certrally enroll --implicit-confirm asks for it, as does openssl cmp -implicit_confirm.

--confirm-wait sets the time the client has to confirm a certificate, sent as confirmWaitTime (default 10s). The CA refuses a later certConf with badRequest and drops a transaction whose certificate is not confirmed in time. certrally enroll --fault late-certconf tests this.

docs.title: Profile checks
docs.text:
--strict refuses requests that break RFC 9483 instead of accepting the usual deviations, such as a missing transactionID, a NULL-DN sender or a reused senderNonce. It also overrides the --accept values that relax a rule of the profile.

--mac-iterations MIN-MAX accepts only shared-secret MACs whose iteration count is in the range. The default is 1 to 500000. Use it with certrally enroll --iterations to test the limits of a client.

--accept NAME (repeatable) accepts one deviation from the profile:

Name Accepts missing-pollreq-nonce a pollReq without recipNonce missing-certconf-nonce a certConf without recipNonce missing-subject a certificate template without subject any-cert-req-id a certReqId other than 0, repeated in the response missing-revocation-reason a revocation request without reason code missing-revocation-issuer a revocation request without issuer poposkinput a signature proof of possession over poposkInput signature-pop no proof of possession in a request signed with a certificate for the key sha1 SHA-1 signatures in the protection and the proof of possession mac-revocation revocation requests not signed with the revoked certificate, such as MAC-protected ones raw-subject the subject as encoded in the request, keeping every attribute, order and string type encrypted-cert-pop the encrypted certificate proof of possession challenge-pop the challenge-response proof of possession

mac-revocation authorizes every such request, because the test CA has no revocation policy of its own. encrypted-cert-pop and challenge-pop serve clients that prove possession without a signature, such as enroll with an ML-KEM key and --pop encrypted-cert or --pop challenge. The test CA certifies an ML-KEM key with keyEncipherment as its only key usage.

certrally mock --strict --mac-iterations 100-10000 --accept sha1

docs.title: Output and colour
docs.text: The message diagram goes to standard error and the summary to standard output. --quiet hides both. --json replaces them with one JSON document, see json.md.

docs.title: Colour
docs.text:
certrally colours its output only when it writes to a terminal. These settings change that, highest priority first:

Setting Effect --color always or --color never Always or never use colour NO_COLOR set to any non-empty value No colour. Bold and other text styles remain on a terminal FORCE_COLOR or CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 Colour even when the output is a pipe or a file. FORCE_COLOR=0 and FORCE_COLOR=false have no effect TERM=dumb No colour

The colour depth comes from TERM and COLORTERM.

docs.title: Existing files
docs.text: certrally does not replace an existing output file, such as --cert-out or --key-out, unless --force is given. On a terminal it asks first, once for all the files that exist, and the default answer is no. Without a terminal, and with --json, it stops with an error instead. The check runs before anything is sent, so a refusal costs no request.

docs.title: Response profiles
docs.text:
certrally checks every CMP response against rules of the Lightweight CMP Profile (RFC 9483) and RFC 9810 that some CAs do not follow. It checks EST responses against rules of RFC 7030 and SCEP responses against rules of RFC 8894 in the same way. --profile chooses what happens when a response breaks one of them:

Profile Effect compatible The default. certrally accepts the response and prints a warning that names the rule strict certrally stops the exchange before it accepts the response and exits with status 6

--profile works with every command that talks to a server. With --json the warnings appear in warnings and the profile in profile.

certrally cacerts --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp --ref device-42 --profile strict

Checks that keep the exchange secure do not depend on the profile. certrally always rejects a response with the wrong transaction ID, a recipient nonce that does not match the request or protection that does not verify.

Some CAs copy the senderKID of a signed request into their signed responses, so it names none of the certificates certrally could check the signature with. compatible then tries each of them. The signer must still chain to a trusted CA certificate and have the sender's name. strict stops such a response.

docs.title: Rejections and enrollment
docs.text:
A rejection from the CA ends the command with exit status 3 in both profiles. Rules that the rejection breaks are listed as warnings, because the reason the CA gives is more useful than the deviation.

When strict stops an ip, cp or kup response, certrally neither confirms nor saves the certificate. Depending on its policy, the CA revokes or keeps a certificate that is never confirmed. When strict stops the pkiconf that answers the confirmation, the CA has already issued and confirmed the certificate, so certrally saves it and exits with status 5.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text: Rule Source pvno is 2 or 3 RFC 9483 section 3.5 senderNonce is present and at least 128 bits long RFC 9483 section 3.5 Only ip, cp and kup carry implicitConfirm in generalInfo RFC 9483 section 3.1 implicitConfirm is granted only when the request asked for it, which enroll --implicit-confirm does RFC 9810 section 5.1.1.1 confirmWaitTime comes with messageTime and never with implicitConfirm RFC 9483 section 3.1 No response carries certProfile RFC 9483 section 3.1 The response is protected the same way as the request: a MAC answers a MAC and a signature answers a signature. Error messages are exempt, because a CA signs them when it cannot check the request RFC 9483 section 3.2 A signed response has a senderKID when its protection certificate has a subject key identifier RFC 9483 section 3.1 The senderKID of a signed response is the subject key identifier of a certificate in extraCerts or among the trusted ones. It counts as broken only when one of those certificates has the sender's name and a subject key identifier RFC 9483 section 3.1 The first signed response of an operation starts extraCerts with its protection certificate, the certificate whose key verifies the signature. Error messages are exempt RFC 9483 section 3.3 An ip, cp or kup that issues a certificate carries extraCerts with the chain of the new certificate. A certificate issued directly by a self-signed CA certificate that certrally trusts or finds in caPubs needs none, because self-signed certificates are left out of extraCerts RFC 9483 section 3.3 An error message has the status rejection. While the CA prepares a certificate the status may be waiting RFC 9483 section 3.6.4 A pkiconf holds an ASN.1 NULL rather than nothing RFC 9810 section 5.3.17

docs.title: EST rules
docs.text:
Rule Source A simpleenroll or simplereenroll response carries only the issued certificate, not its chain RFC 7030 section 4.2.3 A simpleenroll or simplereenroll response has the content type application/pkcs7-mime; smime-type=certs-only RFC 7030 section 4.2.3 The certificate part of a serverkeygen response follows the same two rules RFC 7030 section 4.4.2 A 202 Accepted response to an enrollment request has a Retry-After header RFC 7030 section 4.2.3

With compatible, certrally saves the issued certificate from a response that carries the chain. Without Retry-After it waits 10 seconds before it sends the request again.

An HTTP error from the EST server ends the command with exit status 3 in both profiles. An answer that is not EST at all, such as a redirect, a 404 Not Found or a web page, ends it with exit status 2.

docs.title: SCEP rules
docs.text:
Rule Source A GetCACaps answer holds no control characters, such as a NUL byte, besides the line breaks between capabilities RFC 8894 section 3.5.2 A GetCACert answer with one certificate has the content type application/x-x509-ca-cert, and one with several has application/x-x509-ca-ra-cert RFC 8894 sections 4.2.1.1 and 4.2.1.2 A PKIOperation answer has the content type application/x-pki-message RFC 8894 section 4.3.1 A GetNextCACert answer has the content type application/x-x509-next-ca-cert RFC 8894 section 4.7.1 A CertRep has a senderNonce attribute RFC 8894 section 3.2.1

With compatible, certrally drops control characters around each capability and accepts the answer. certrally checks only answers that have content and either HTTP status 200 or a CertRep.

A FAILURE answer ends the command with exit status 3 in both profiles, and so does an HTTP error status such as 503 Service Unavailable once the retries are used up. An answer without content, a redirect, a 404 Not Found or a web page ends it with exit status 2.

docs.title: Checking recorded runs
docs.text:
certrally lint applies the same rules to responses recorded with --capture or saved as message files. It exits with status 6 when a response breaks a rule and with 0 when none does.

certrally lint run.jsonl

Each response is checked as the answer to the request before it in the same run. Messages from other files form one exchange in command line order, such as certrally lint ir.der ip.der certConf.der pkiconf.der. Without --ca-cert the certificates in the first response of each exchange count as trusted, as they do during a run.

An EST or SCEP response is checked on its own, without its request. These rules concern the HTTP response, so lint checks only EST and SCEP responses in capture files and skips EST message files.

lint also checks what certrally enforces during a CMP run, because messages from other clients have not been through those checks: each response carries the transactionID of its request (RFC 9483 section 3.1) and a recipNonce equal to the senderNonce of its request or, for a delayed response, of an earlier request of the same transaction (RFC 9483 section 3.5).

docs.title: Enroll over SCEP
docs.text:
The certrally scep commands talk to a SCEP server, usually over plain HTTP. --server is the SCEP URL of the server, such as http://scep.example.com/scep. A server with several CAs needs the name of the CA in --ca.

Command What it does scep caps Lists the capabilities of the server and the algorithms certrally picks from them scep cacert Gets the CA and RA certificates. --fingerprint and --out save them scep chain Gets the CA certificate and the certificates that issued it scep nextca Gets the CA certificate that will replace the current one scep enroll Requests a certificate for a new key, --new-key or --csr scep renew Renews the certificate in --cert scep poll Collects a certificate that the CA kept pending scep getcert, scep getcrl Get a certificate by its serial number or the CRL that covers a certificate scep mock Runs a SCEP test CA on your machine 
certrally scep enroll --server http://scep.example.com/scep --ca 'Issuing CA' --ca-cert ca.pem \
  --challenge-file challenge.txt --subject CN=device-42 \
  --cert-out device.pem --key-out device.key

Over plain HTTP nothing authenticates the first GetCACert answer, so save the CA certificates once with scep cacert --fingerprint and pass them with --ca-cert. The challenge password comes from --challenge, --challenge-file or CERTRALLY_CHALLENGE. When the CA answers PENDING, certrally keeps polling and saves the request in a state file that scep poll continues. The sections below describe trust, the challenge password, algorithms, pending requests, renewal, queries and the scep mock test CA. Key files, encrypted keys and --out-format der work as for CMP, see keys.md.

docs.title: Server address and CA name
docs.text:
--server is the SCEP URL of the server, such as http://scep.example.com/scep. certrally adds the operation and message query parameters of RFC 8894 section 4.1.

A server that serves several CAs needs the name of the CA in --ca, which certrally sends as the message parameter of GetCACert, GetCACertChain, GetNextCACert and GetCACaps. Some servers answer GetCACert without content when the name is missing or unknown. certrally then exits with status 2 and suggests --ca. A 404 Not Found usually means a wrong path in --server, but some servers also answer it for a CA name they do not serve. Some answer it to GetNextCACert when they have no next CA certificate.

docs.title: Trusting the CA
docs.text:
SCEP signs and encrypts its messages itself, so it often runs over plain HTTP. Nothing then authenticates the first GetCACert answer. Commands without --ca-cert trust the certificates of that answer and warn about it.

Check the CA once and save it for later commands:

certrally scep cacert --server http://scep.example.com/scep --ca 'Issuing CA'
certrally scep cacert --server http://scep.example.com/scep --ca 'Issuing CA' \
  --fingerprint 9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08 --out ca.pem

scep cacert shows each certificate with its SHA-256 and SHA-1 fingerprints and its role: the issuing CA, an RA that decrypts requests or an RA that signs answers. --fingerprint takes a SHA-256 or SHA-1 fingerprint in hex, with or without colons. The certificate with that fingerprint is saved together with the certificates it issued, such as RA certificates. The other certificates of the answer are listed and not saved. Later commands trust the saved file with --ca-cert and do not send GetCACert. --fingerprint on the other commands checks the GetCACert answer before the request is sent.

scep chain sends GetCACertChain, which RFC 8894 does not define but some servers offer. It shows the CA certificate followed by the certificates that issued it, in the order of the server. --fingerprint and --out work as for scep cacert, so the fingerprint of the root saves the whole chain.

Over HTTPS the server certificate is checked against the system roots or --tls-ca-cert. --insecure skips that check for a test server.

docs.title: Challenge password
docs.text:
A PKCSReq carries a challenge password that authorizes the request. It comes from --challenge, --challenge-file (- reads standard input) or the CERTRALLY_CHALLENGE environment variable, in that order. certrally never asks for it, because many servers need none. Other users of the machine can see --challenge in the process list. Some servers also check the challenge password in a RenewalReq, so scep renew accepts the same flags.

Some servers refuse a missing or wrong challenge password with an HTTP error such as 400 Bad Request or 403 Forbidden instead of a FAILURE answer. Some do the same for a subject they do not know. certrally exits with status 3, shows the text of the error page and suggests checking the challenge password, --subject and --ca.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
Before a PKIOperation certrally sends GetCACaps and picks the algorithms from the answer:

Choice Default Flag Signature digest SHA-256, or SHA-512 or SHA-1 when the server lists one of them and not SHA-256 --hash: sha256, sha384, sha512, sha1 or md5 Content cipher AES-128-CBC, or DES-EDE3-CBC when the server lists DES3 and not AES --cipher: aes128, aes192, aes256, des3 or des HTTP method POST when the server lists POSTPKIOperation, GET otherwise

A server that lists SCEPStandard gets SHA-256, AES-128-CBC and POST. scep caps shows the capabilities and these choices.

--hash also sets the signature digest of the PKCS#10 request that scep enroll and scep renew create. Without --hash or with md5, which Go does not sign requests with, the request is signed with SHA-256 for an RSA key and with the digest that matches the curve for an ECDSA key. A request from --csr is sent as it is.

certrally signs a PKCSReq with a self-signed certificate for the request key, or for a temporary RSA key when the request key is not RSA, because SCEP encrypts answers to the signer key. The transaction ID is the SHA-1 hash of the public key in uppercase hex, so a request for the same key always has the same ID.

Requests are encrypted with RSA for the RA certificates, or for the CA certificate when the CA has no RA. When one of them has another key type, certrally stops before it sends the request and says that the CA needs an RSA RA certificate.

certrally decrypts answers encrypted with AES or DES-EDE3-CBC and always with the cipher of its request. Some servers encrypt their answers with single DES whatever the request used. certrally then exits with status 4 and suggests --allow-des, which accepts them. Single DES offers no real protection for the certificate, but the certificate is public.

docs.title: Waiting for the CA
docs.text:
A CA that an operator must approve answers PENDING. scep enroll and scep renew then send CertPoll every --poll-interval (default 30 seconds) until the CA issues or rejects the certificate, within --timeout (default 5 minutes). --poll-later stops at the first PENDING answer. Some servers send a PENDING answer with HTTP 202 Accepted and a FAILURE answer with 400 Bad Request. certrally reads the CertRep whatever the HTTP status.

A request that is still pending is saved in a state file, by default the --cert-out file name with .state appended, or the file in --state. It holds the request, the certificate that signs it, the temporary signer key when there is one, the CA certificates and the output file names. It never holds the challenge password. It is written with mode 0600 and removed once the CA decides. At the end of --timeout, certrally keeps the state file and exits with status 2.

certrally scep poll --state device.pem.state

scep poll continues the request from the state file and saves the certificate where the enrollment would have. --once sends a single CertPoll. --server, --ca and --allow-des replace the values of the state file.

docs.title: Renewal
docs.text:
scep renew sends a RenewalReq signed with the certificate in --cert and its key in --key, which must be RSA. The request repeats the subject and subjectAltName of the certificate. A new key is generated unless --new-key or --csr supplies one. The server must list Renewal in its capabilities. certrally warns when it does not.

Servers that follow the drafts before RFC 8894 renew through a PKCSReq signed with the current certificate. Some of them list Renewal and still answer a RenewalReq with FAILURE and badCertId. scep renew --pkcsreq sends such a PKCSReq, signed with --cert and --key and with the same subject and subjectAltName. The server need not list Renewal. PENDING answers and the state file work as for a RenewalReq.

certrally scep renew --server http://scep.example.com/scep --pkcsreq \
  --cert device.pem --key device.key --cert-out device-new.pem --key-out device-new.key

docs.title: Certificates and CRLs from the CA
docs.text:
scep getcert --serial gets a certificate the CA issued, by its serial number in decimal, 0x hex or colon-separated hex. The issuer is the CA certificate unless --issuer names another. scep getcrl gets the CRL for the certificate in --cert or for --serial and checks its signature against the CA certificate.

Both requests are signed with --cert and --key, which servers usually require to be a certificate the CA issued, or else with a temporary self-signed certificate. Some servers answer these message types or RenewalReq without content when they do not support them. certrally then exits with status 2 and says so.

scep nextca sends GetNextCACert and shows the CA and RA certificates that will replace the current ones. The answer must be signed by the current CA or RA.

Many servers have no next CA certificate until a CA key rollover is prepared. RFC 8894 does not say how a server answers then. certrally reports no next CA certificate and exits with status 0 when the server answers without content or answers 404 Not Found while GetCACert works at the same address. Servers built on go-pki-scep answer 404. With --ca-cert certrally sends GetCACert after the 404, so a wrong path or CA name still exits with status 2. Other servers refuse the request with 403 Forbidden or 500 Internal Server Error or lack the operation. certrally exits with status 3 for those, as interop.md lists.

docs.title: Busy servers
docs.text: A server under load may answer HTTP 503. certrally sends the request again up to --busy-retries times (default 3, 0 for never), after the time in the Retry-After header or after --busy-wait (default 5 seconds) when the header is missing.

docs.title: Proxies
docs.text: --proxy takes an http, https or socks5 URL. Without it, the HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY environment variables apply as for CMP.

docs.title: Test CA
docs.text:
certrally scep mock runs a SCEP test CA on 127.0.0.1:8090 and prints commands that work against it. The printed scep enroll command gives the challenge password with --challenge, names the file of --challenge-file and leaves out a challenge from CERTRALLY_CHALLENGE. It answers GetCACaps, GetCACert, GetCACertChain and PKIOperation with PKCSReq, RenewalReq, CertPoll, GetCert and GetCRL over plain HTTP. Everything it issues lives in memory.

Flag Effect --challenge, --challenge-file The challenge password a PKCSReq must carry. Without them and CERTRALLY_CHALLENGE, a random one is generated and printed --any-challenge Issues whatever challenge password a request carries --ca-name Answers GetCACert only for this CA name --ra Decrypts requests and signs answers with a separate RA certificate --next-ca Announces a next CA certificate through GetNextCACert --pending-polls N Answers every new request with PENDING and issues the certificate at the Nth CertPoll --busy-interval Answers HTTP 503 without Retry-After to a PKIOperation sent within this time of the previous one --caps Replaces the GetCACaps answer, such as SHA-1,DES3 for an old CA --ca-out Saves the GetCACert certificates for --ca-cert

The mock prints a line for each request with the operation, the message type, the answer and the reason for a refusal.

docs.title: JSON output
docs.text:
--json prints the outcome as one JSON document on standard output instead of the diagram and the report. The document holds the exit status, every message of the exchange, the result of the command and any error:

certrally cacerts --server https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp --ref device-42 --json \
  | jq -r '.result.certificates[].subject'

--capture run.jsonl appends every message of the run, with its bytes, to a JSON Lines file that inspect and lint read. Keep capture files private, because the messages of a shared-secret exchange allow offline guessing of the secret.

JSON output and capture files describes both formats.

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text: Status Meaning 0 Success 1 Invalid command line or local error, such as an unreadable file 2 The server could not be reached, did not answer in time or did not answer with CMP, EST or SCEP 3 The CA rejected the request, or the EST or SCEP server refused it or the sign-in 4 The response broke the protocol or failed verification 5 The CA issued the certificate but the confirmation failed. certrally saves the certificate. Check with the CA before retrying, because a retry can issue a second certificate 6 A response broke a rule of --profile strict, or lint found a response that breaks a rule

docs.title: Verify a download
docs.text:
Every release is signed and carries build provenance and SBOMs. The commands below check version 0.1.0. Replace the version for other releases.

checksums.txt lists the SHA-256 digest of every archive. The release workflow signs it with a keyless cosign signature. Check the signature, then the archives:

cosign verify-blob --bundle checksums.txt.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity https://github.com/misiektoja/certrally/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v0.1.0 \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com checksums.txt
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt

Archives and images also carry GitHub build provenance:

gh attestation verify certrally_0.1.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz --repo misiektoja/certrally
gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/misiektoja/certrally:0.1.0 --repo misiektoja/certrally

The release also carries the archive provenance as certrally_0.1.0.intoto.jsonl, for gh attestation verify --bundle without access to GitHub's API.

Each archive has an SPDX SBOM next to it, named after the archive with .sbom.json appended. The image carries its SBOM as an attestation.
